title: Modals and semi-modals
subtitle: Ability, permission, advice, criticism, obligation, degrees of certainty

items: The nine main modals (**will, would, can, could, may, might, shall, should, must**) have only one form (they do not change tense or person) and are followed by a simple or continuous bare infinitive (e.g. **could + do, be doing, have done, have been doing**). They can also be followed by a bare infinitive in the passive (e.g. **could + be done, have been done**).
Semi-modals have similar meanings to modals. They include: **need (to), ought to, had better, have (got) to**.
Some semi-modals, such as **had better**, do not change tense or person. Others, such as **have (got) to**, do.
Some semi-modals can be used in combination with modals, producing phrases such as **might have to**.

rows.example: You **can't** really **speak** seven languages fluently, **can** you?
There's no way you **could read** when you were two!

rows.use: Real ability · decisions made now about future ability
rows.example: I **can get** you a paper when I go to the shop, if you like.
One day, maybe, all adults **will be able to** read and write.
I **couldn't go** on a quiz show. I'd be too scared!
I **could go** with them to the cinema tomorrow but I won't because I've already seen the film.
They **could have asked** the Prime Minister much more searching questions. I wonder why they didn't.

blocks.text: The full negative form of modals is written as two words, e.g. **could not**. The exception is **cannot**, which is one word.
**Can** and **could** cannot be used as infinitives. We use **be able to** instead.
blocks.note: I'd love **to be able to** come with you to the cinema tomorrow but I just can't.

blocks.text: We don't usually use **could** for past ability on one occasion. We use **was/were able to, managed to, succeeded**, etc. However, with verbs such as **see, hear, feel**, etc. we can use **could** for past ability on one occasion.
blocks.note: Luckily, she **was able to** finish the article in time. · I **could see** that she was tired.

rows.example: **Can** I finish watching this before I go to bed?
No, you **can't**.

blocks.text: **May** is more polite and formal than **could**, and **could** is more polite and formal than **can**.
We don't usually use modals to talk about past permission. We can use **was/were allowed to**.
blocks.note: We **were allowed to** buy one comic each. However, we do use **could** to talk about past permission in reported speech: Mum said we **could** buy one comic each.

rows.example: You **should** try to get that poem published.

blocks.text: We can only use **had better** in questions.
blocks.note: **Hadn't you better** check that these facts are actually true?

blocks.text: We can also use **might/may as well** to give advice and make suggestions. This suggests that, although the suggestion is not perfect, there is no better option.
blocks.note: We **may as well** watch this as there's nothing else on.

rows.example: You **shouldn't have spoken** to Mrs Todd like that.
You **could/might have told** me you were going to be late!
He **will slam** the door every time he goes out.

rows.use: Criticising a specific example of someone's general behaviour
rows.example: You **would take** the car just when I wanted to go out.

blocks.text: We can also use **might as well** to suggest criticism.
blocks.note: I **might as well** be dead for all you care.

rows.example: You **have to** be a good communicator to be a press spokesperson.

rows.use: A lack of current or general obligation
rows.example: You **don't always need to** have a degree to become a journalist.
You'll **have to** do quite a lot of research before you write this report.
I'm glad we **won't have to** write any more essays on this course.
We **had to** come up with three questions each.
In the past, politicians **didn't have to** deal with being in a 24-hour media spotlight.

blocks.text: We are more likely to use **must** for personal obligation (making our own decision about what we must do) and **have to** for external obligation (someone else making a decision about what we must do).
Using **must** for questions is extremely formal. We usually use **have to**.
blocks.note: **Do you have to** have a degree to be a journalist?

blocks.text: **Mustn't** is used for prohibition. **Don't have to** is used for a lack of obligation.
We can use **didn't have to** and **didn't need to** for things that we did or didn't actually do. However, we only use **needn't have done** for things that we actually did but weren't obliged to.
blocks.note: We **needn't have printed** twenty copies — ten would have been enough. (we did print twenty)

rows.use: Certainty (or near certainty) about now, the future or generally
rows.example: 'There's someone at the door.' 'That'll be the postman.' · 'It **can't** be. He's already been.'

rows.use: Certainty (or near certainty) about the past
rows.example: 'They **won't have heard** the news, will they?' 'They **must have heard** by now, surely.'

rows.use: Probability about now, the future or generally
rows.example: 'The weather **should** be good tomorrow, shouldn't it?' 'Actually, the forecast said it **may well rain**.'
'Jan **should have finished** writing her article by now, shouldn't she?' 'She **may well have done**, but I haven't seen it yet.'

rows.use: Possibility about now, the future or generally
rows.example: I **might (just) have** time to get to the library before it closes.
Jim **might not have checked** his e-mail yet.

blocks.text: **should** and **should have** can be used in that clauses after words expressing importance and reactions.
blocks.note: It's strange that you **should say** that. · Was it necessary that Alan **should have been invited** to the meeting?

exercises.title: A · Circle the correct phrase
exercises.instruction: Select the form that fits. If both forms are possible, choose the option that says both.

items.prompt: You ___ really talk when you were one year old, ___ you?
We ___ give you a lift home tonight, if you want.
I wish I ___ speak Russian, then I'd be able to / I could read Tolstoy in the original.
Excuse me, ___ you tell me how to get to the leisure centre from here?
I'm afraid we ___ be able to come to the wedding after all.
Thankfully, we ___ get to the airport just in time so we didn't miss the plane.
Dawn ___ gone to the barbecue as she had to work.
Would you like to ___ buy the flat you're renting?
In a thousand years, ___ travel faster than the speed of light?
options: both: can humans / will humans be able to

items.prompt: 'Mum, can I watch TV and do my homework later?' 'No, you ___ not!'
We could catch / have caught the last train after all, but of course we didn't know that at the time.
options: both: could catch / could have caught

items.prompt: ___ I at least stay up till the end of the film?
Everyone ___ tell that Julie was upset about something.
___ I open the window, please? It's a little stuffy in here.
Because we had guests last Saturday, the kids ___ stay up till midnight.

exercises.title: B · Verb box
exercises.instruction: Write a verb from the box in the correct form in each gap.

items.prompt: It seems there's nothing anybody can ___ to stop the conflict escalating further.
She couldn't ___ anything in her left arm for about two hours. She said it was completely numb.
I don't think the Prime Minister will ever manage ___ from this scandal.
Can I ___ Tracy round after tea? We want to play my new computer game.
Liz has had another ice cream so why can't I ___ one? It's not fair!
When I was a child, my brothers and sisters and I weren't allowed ___ with the grown-ups except on special occasions.
Darren's allergic to wheat, so he can't ___ bread under any circumstances.
Dominic had said he spoke German, but when we got there it turned out he couldn't ___ a word.
I'd love to be able ___ from home, but in my job it's just not possible.
James could ___ for Parliament at the last election — he had enough support — but he wasn't willing to sacrifice his privacy.
A small cot for babies can ___ if you ask at reception.
We couldn't ___ to the concert anyway as Jamie wasn't very well.

exercises.title: C · Tick or rewrite
exercises.instruction: If the word in bold is correct, write a tick (✓). If it is incorrect, rewrite it correctly.

items.prompt: **Shouldn't** you **getting** planning permission before you start building?
Gavin really ought not **to be worn** casual clothes to the interview last week.
She might have **gave** us a call to let us know she **was** all right.
You **should better** get a second opinion before you do anything drastic like knock down a supporting wall.
I don't think you **must** go to school today if you're not feeling well.
We definitely **should not** judge Karen until we know exactly what happened.
I probably won't get the job but I **should** as well apply for it, I suppose.
You **could have told** us you'd changed your mind about the holiday. How are we going to find a fourth person at this late stage?
We had **rather** book the tickets now, hadn't we? They might have sold out on the day.
Terry **would** leave his bedroom in such a mess all the time. It's just not good enough.
Michael was late, but then again he **will** be.
You **may have asked** me if I wanted to come with you! You know I need to go to the bank!

exercises.title: D · Similar meaning
exercises.instruction: Write a word or short phrase in each gap so that the second sentence has a similar meaning to the first sentence.

items.prompt:
I would suggest seeing a doctor if it doesn't clear up.
You had ___ a doctor if it doesn't clear up.

It was typical of Jerry to forget to feed the cat, wasn't it?
Jerry ___ to feed the cat, ___ he?

I'm annoyed Diana didn't invite us to her engagement party.
Diana ___ us to her engagement party.

Buying a yellow car was a mistake — everyone thinks I drive a taxi!
I ___ a yellow car — everyone thinks I drive a taxi!

Teenagers are noisy, aren't they?
Teenagers ___ make so much noise, ___ they?

It won't harm us to see what special offers are on at the moment.
We ___ what special offers are on at the moment.

Don't you think you should type that essay, rather than write it in pen?
___ better type that essay, rather than write it in pen?

It would probably have been a good idea if you'd asked Dad what he thought.
You ___ Dad what he thought.

exercises.title: E · Obligation words
exercises.instruction: Write a word from the box in each gap. You will need two of the words twice.

items.prompt: I ___ have bothered preparing so much food; nobody ate anything anyway.
Do you ___ to have that music on so loud? I can't concentrate!
You ___ call before you come round, as we'll definitely be in.
It was difficult, but I knew I ___ to apologise.
Trisha ___ need to get a summer job as her parents are quite well-off.
___ you have to be taken in court yourself, or can a lawyer represent you?
We didn't ___ to wear a uniform to school today, so I went in jeans and a T-shirt.
I think Damien ___ to stay in hospital for the next four or five weeks.
Children ___ not be left unattended under any circumstances.
We haven't ___ to move out for another six months, but we've started looking for a new place anyway.

exercises.title: F · must, have to, need
exercises.instruction: Complete using must, have to, need or need to in the correct form and the correct form of the words in brackets.

items.prompt: You ___ me back now, but of course you can if you like! (pay)
Dogs ___ on a leash at all times. (keep)
If Linda ___ from school tomorrow, maybe we could spend the afternoon in town. (pick up)
acceptedAnswers: doesn't have to be picked up
doesn't need to be picked up

items.prompt: We ___ on phone lines in the future as we'll all have mobile phones that connect to the Internet. (rely)
The invitations ___ soon otherwise they won't get there in time. (send off)
Sorry I'm late. I ___ a few things from the supermarket on my way here. (get)
___ a fuss to get your money back, or was the manager quite reasonable? (you / make)
You ___ everything Graham tells you. He's lied to me before. (believe)
Thankfully we ___ Flossie in a cattery as our neighbours offered to feed her. (put)
What time ___ every morning? (farmers / get up)
acceptedAnswers: do farmers have to get up

items.prompt: I'd hate ___ to work every morning and evening, wouldn't you? (commute)
Although we took CDs with us we actually ___ as there was no CD player to play them on. (do)

exercises.title: G · Cloze: A tabloid editor speaks
exercises.instruction: Write one word in each gap.

items.prompt: It is my job to tell the readers when a celebrity has done something they should not have ___.
Or when a politician ___ to have done something but didn't.
One accusation that is often levelled at tabloids is that we think we ___ not need to worry about the truth, but that is just not true.
As a newspaper, you have ___ to get your facts right.
And you ___ not print a story just because you want it to be true.
There are times when, in retrospect, we ___ not have been so careful and could have broken a story days before we did.
But we ___ to have absolute proof first.
They realise they might as ___ put their side of the story across.
They know they ___ definitely have to speak out at some point, so why wait?
Celebrities need to ___ talked about constantly or they stop being famous.
So they ___ not complain, in my view.
You ___ not fear us if you haven't done anything wrong.
But if you have, you ___ better look out, because we are going to catch you.

exercises.title: H · Circle the correct phrase
exercises.instruction: Select the form that fits. If both forms are possible, choose the option that says both.

items.prompt: 'Did you hear a noise?' '___ the cat.'
'I had to walk all the way here.' 'You must be / have been exhausted. Put your feet up. I'll make us a nice cup of tea.'
options: both: must be / must have been

items.prompt: 'Your favourite programme's on.' 'It mustn't / can't be. It's only half past five.'
'Andy made me redo every single one of the reports.' 'You must / can have been furious.'
'Laura walked right past me in the street without saying a word.' 'She can't / couldn't have seen you.'
'I can't believe I got the final question in the pop quiz wrong.' 'Don't worry. I wouldn't / won't have known the answer either.'
'I can't wait to get that blue top tomorrow.' 'I wouldn't get too excited. They only had one left, so they may / might well have sold out.'
'It's got very cold.' 'Yes, I think it must / might easily snow tonight.'
'I can't wait till Roger gets here!' 'He should land / have landed by now, so he'll be here in about an hour.'
options: both: should land / should have landed

items.prompt: 'I hope they've got some tickets left.' 'We should / might just be lucky and get the last two.'

exercises.title: I · Key-word transformations
exercises.instruction: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between three and eight words, including the word given.

items.prompt:
It's possible that Greg didn't go to Swansea after all. **not**
Greg ___ to Swansea after all.

It's quite likely that Sasha was lying about what Doug said. **well**
Sasha ___ about what Doug said.

The most likely situation is that they awarded Grandpa the medal during the war. **must**
Grandpa ___ during the war.
acceptedAnswers: must have been awarded the medal

items.prompt:
I'd be surprised if Derek has already arrived. **ought**
Derek ___ yet.

Jake, is it definite that they haven't announced the winner yet? **will**
Jake, ___ announced yet?

It's highly likely that Stephen was listening. **may**
Stephen ___ listening.

It's not possible that Andrew is half Spanish. **be**
Andrew ___ half Spanish.

___ Eliot better tell his mum what happened?
